title: Variables, constants, inputs and outputs
specPoints: 2.2.1 Programming fundamentals: the use of **variables**, **constants**, **operators**, **inputs**, **outputs** and **assignments**
Practical programming skills: write and run code that stores data, takes input and produces output
learn: Explain what a variable is and choose sensible names
Assign values with `=` and update a variable from its old value
Explain the difference between a variable and a constant and when to use each
Take keyboard input with `input()` and show output with `print()`, in OCR pseudocode and in Python
Read a short program and state what it outputs
hook: Three boxes on the desk labelled `name`, `age`, `score`. I put a card in each. Now I take the card out of `age`, write a bigger number, put it back. Did the box change? Did its name change? A variable is a labelled box. Everything else today is what you can do with boxes.

video.title: Variables: boxes with names
video.brief: 3 minutes. Animated boxes: `score = 0` creates a box; `score = score + 10` shows the right-hand side evaluated first, then the result dropped into the box. Then a `PI = 3.14159` box with a padlock: constant. Then `input()` as a hand posting a card into a box, `print()` as the box's contents appearing on a screen. End with the four lines of pseudocode and the same four lines of Python side by side.

p: A **variable** is a named location in memory that holds a value which can change while the program runs. You create one by **assigning** a value with `=`. The right-hand side is worked out first, then stored in the name on the left — so `score = score + 10` means 'take the current score, add 10, store the result back in score'.
explain.code:
score = 0
score = score + 10
name = "Ada"
print(name + " has " + str(score))

p: Names should say what the value is: `total_price`, `is_logged_in`, `attempts`. Not `x`, `thing`, `var1`. Exam mark schemes award a mark for *meaningful identifiers* in longer programming questions, and in 2.3 you will see it listed under maintainability.

A **constant** is a named value that is set once and never changes while the program runs: `VAT_RATE = 0.2`, `MAX_PLAYERS = 4`. Written in CAPITALS by convention. Use a constant when a value appears in several places and must stay the same: change it once at the top and the whole program updates. OCR pseudocode writes `const VAT_RATE = 0.2`.

`input()` pauses, shows a message, and returns what the user typed — always as **text** (a string), even if they type a number. `print()` shows a value on screen. Joining text uses `+`; numbers must be converted to text first with `str()`, and text to numbers with `int()` or `float()` (more in lesson 6).
explain.code:
OCR pseudocode                   Python
--------------                   ------
name = input("Name? ")           name = input("Name? ")
age = int(input("Age? "))        age = int(input("Age? "))
print("Hi " + name)              print("Hi " + name)
print(age + 1)                   print(age + 1)

p: Half the Paper 2 marks on this topic are 'state the output'. Work line by line, keep a note of each variable, and remember that `=` **replaces** what was in the box.

simple.h: A variable is a box with a name
p: `score = 0` makes a box called `score` with 0 in it. `score = score + 10` means: look in the box (0), add 10, put 10 back in the box. The `=` sign means **put this in the box**, not 'equals'.
`total_price` is a good name. `x` is a bad name. Good names get marks.

simple.h: A constant is a box you lock
p: `VAT_RATE = 0.2` is set once and never changes. Write it in CAPITALS.
`input("Name? ")` asks the user and gives you what they typed, as text. `print(...)` shows something on screen.

keyterms.def: A named memory location holding a value that can change while the program runs.
A named value that cannot change while the program runs.
Storing a value in a variable using `=`.
Data entered into the program, e.g. from the keyboard.
Data the program shows or sends out, e.g. to the screen.
The name given to a variable, constant or subprogram.

try.title: 1. Run it, then change it
p: Run this. Then change it so it also asks for the user's favourite subject and prints a sentence using all three values.
try.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print("Hello " + name)
print("Next year you will be " + str(age + 1))

try.title: 2. Predict, then run
p: Before you press Run, write down what you think this prints. Then run it. Were you right about line 4?
try.code:
a = 5
b = a
a = a + 1
print(a, b)
b = b * 2
print(a, b)

p: A shop adds 20% VAT. Finish the program using the constant, and make it ask for the price.

price = float(input("Price before VAT: "))
# work out the VAT and the total

opts: Causes an error — you cannot join text and a number

exam.q: State what is meant by a **variable** in a program.
model: A named location in memory / identifier whose value can change while the program is running (1).
exam.commentary: 'Stores a value' alone is borderline; add 'can change' or 'named'. One sentence.

exam.q: A program uses the value 9.81 in several calculations. Explain why it should be stored as a **constant**.
model: The value does not change during the program, so a constant prevents it being altered by mistake (1). If it needs changing later it is changed in one place and the whole program updates / the name makes the code easier to read than a bare number (1).
exam.commentary: Two different reasons needed: protection from accidental change, and maintainability/readability. Repeating one reason in two ways scores one.

exam.q: Write a program that asks the user for the length and width of a rectangle and outputs its area.
model: Two inputs stored in variables, converted to numbers (1). Area calculated as length × width (1). Area output (1).

length = int(input("Length: "))
width = int(input("Width: "))
area = length * width
print(area)
exam.commentary: Pseudocode or Python both fine. The usual lost mark is forgetting `int()` — in Python that makes `*` fail; in OCR pseudocode examiners are lenient on casting in short questions, but it costs nothing to include.

home: Write a program that asks for a person's name, their year of birth and the current year, then prints a sentence saying how old they are this year. Use a meaningful name for every variable. Test it in the Python IDE.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 5 · explain 10 · try 28 · check 5 · exam 9 · homework 3
misconceptions: `=` read as mathematical equality, so `x = x + 1` looks 'impossible'. The box model fixes this — do it physically.
Expecting `b` to change when `a` changes after `b = a` (Try 2 targets this).
Believing `input()` gives a number. Let the error happen in Try 1 by removing `int()`.
Single-letter names. Model good names in every example on the board.
say: 'Right side first. Then into the box.'
'Say the name out loud. If it doesn't tell you what's inside, rename it.'
teacher.skip: Try 4 and 5 are optional; Try 1–3 with the in-page runner is the core.
differentiation: Support: give Try 3 with the two calculation lines present but the right-hand sides blank.
Stretch: ask for the VAT program to use a second constant for a discount percentage and show the maths for both.
